items.title: Code of Practice for the Cyber Security of AI
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.quote: an audit log of changes to system prompts or other model configuration (including prompts) that affect the underlying working of the systems
items.why: Source of the quotation (provision 8.3, a 'should', addressed to developers). Provision 6.1: developers and operators shall evaluate access control frameworks and secure APIs, models, data and pipelines. 6.3: dedicated environments with least privilege. 12.1: operators shall log system and user actions. 7.4: operators shall tell end-users before models are updated. Voluntary.

items.title: ETSI TS 104 223 V1.1.1: Securing Artificial Intelligence (SAI); Baseline Cyber Security Requirements for AI Models and Systems
items.quote: identify appropriate measures to secure APIs, models, data, and training and processing pipelines
items.why: The international specification carrying the same access control and audit log provisions as the UK Code. A specification, not law.

items.title: Guidelines for secure AI system development: Secure deployment
items.locator: Sections 'Secure your infrastructure' and 'Protect your model continuously'
items.quote: You apply appropriate access controls to your APIs, models and data, and to their training and processing pipelines
items.why: Says access control applies in research and development as well as in deployment, and warns that attackers may tamper with models, data or prompts during or after training. Guidance, not a rule.

items.title: Guidelines for secure AI system development: Secure development
items.locator: Section 'Identify, track and protect your assets'
items.quote: You have processes and tools to track, authenticate, version control and secure your assets
items.why: Lists the assets that count: models, data, prompts, software, documentation and logs, and says logs themselves are sensitive. Basis for treating a prompt as an asset under version control.

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 32: Security of processing
items.quote: who has access to personal data does not process them except on instructions from the controller
items.why: The binding rule where personal data is involved: security appropriate to the risk, including the risk of unauthorised alteration or access, and a duty to ensure people with access act only on instructions. Not specific to AI and silent on prompts and models as such.

items.title: Cyber Essentials: Requirements for IT infrastructure v3.2
items.locator: Section 4 'User access control', pp. 19-20
items.quote: Your organisation must be in control of your user accounts and the access privileges that allow access to your organisational data and services.
items.why: The government-backed baseline: accounts only for authorised individuals, unique credentials, and special care with administrative accounts. Not written for AI, but the platforms on which prompts and models are edited are ordinary accounts within its scope. Certification is voluntary.

items.title: Implementation Guide for the AI Cyber Security Code of Practice
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.locator: Provision 5.4, PDF p. 27, 'Implement Strong Data Access Controls'
items.quote: Programmatic updates via pipelines have strict RBAC and approvals in place to prevent abuse.
items.why: The only source read that speaks of approval before a change lands, and only for automated pipeline updates. Explanatory, not a requirement.

items.title: Poisoning Attacks on LLMs Require a Near-constant Number of Poison Samples
items.locator: Abstract on the AI Security Institute research page
items.quote: 250 poisoned documents similarly compromise models across all model and dataset sizes
items.why: Source of the figure. Models from 600 million to 13 billion parameters; the same dynamics were shown for fine-tuning. Why control over who can add to training and fine-tuning data matters: the number of documents needed does not grow with the model. Only the abstract on the Institute's page was read.

items.title: LLM07:2025 System Prompt Leakage
items.locator: Description
items.quote: the system prompt should not be considered a secret, nor should it be used as a security control
items.why: Warns against putting credentials or permission rules in a prompt: access must be enforced outside the model. Community consensus document, not a standard. No publication date is shown on the page.

items.title: Guidance on AI and data protection: How should we assess security and data minimisation in AI?
items.locator: Section 'How should we ensure training data is secure?'
items.quote: Your technical teams should record and document all movements and storing of personal data from one location to another.
items.why: The data protection regulator on audit trails for training data. The page carries a banner that the guidance is under review following the Data (Use and Access) Act.

items.title: Bates and Others v Post Office Limited (No 6: Horizon Issues) [2019] EWHC 3408 (QB)
items.publisher: High Court of Justice, Queen's Bench Division (Courts and Tribunals Judiciary)
items.locator: Paras 1007-1013 (answers to Horizon Issues 11 and 12), PDF pp. 308-309
items.quote: the roles were very wide and in my judgment they were not controlled
items.why: The court's finding on privileged access in the Post Office Horizon system: the supplier's staff could alter branch data remotely, the powerful roles were not controlled, and proper logs were not kept, so nobody could say how often data had been changed. The clearest UK finding of what uncontrolled, unlogged access costs the people a system decides about. A judgment about an accounting system, not AI; a very long document, of which the Horizon Issues on remote access and their answers were read.

items.title: Penalty Notice: Capita plc and Capita Pension Solutions Limited
items.locator: Para 7(iii), PDF p. 7; paras 80 and 90 on privileged access management
items.quote: failed to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to prevent both privilege escalation and unauthorised lateral movement through the network
items.why: An enforcement decision that turns on privileged access: the regulator found the companies had not prevented privilege escalation, in breach of the security duties in UK GDPR, and judged them against privileged access management, tiered administrator accounts and the principle of least privilege. Shows that weak control of privileged accounts is treated as a breach of Article 32 in its own right. Not about AI; a published version with redactions; the companies settled and made full admissions.

items.title: Data Protection Act 2018, section 62: Logging
items.quote: so far as possible, the identity of the person who consulted the data
items.why: The one UK statutory duty found that requires a log of who did what in an automated system: collection, alteration, consultation, disclosure, combination and erasure. It applies only to law enforcement processing by competent authorities under Part 3 of the Act, so it binds police and similar bodies, not business generally. Amended by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 from 19 August 2025, which removed the duty to record the reason for consulting or disclosing data. legislation.gov.uk shows it up to date to 4 October 2026.

items.title: SS1/23 Model risk management principles for banks
items.locator: Principle 2.3 'Policies and procedures', item (c)(viii), PDF p. 17; Principle 3.3(c) on testing material model changes
items.quote: approval and monitoring procedures that need to be followed when a material change is made to a model
items.why: A UK regulator's expectation of change control for models: named approval authorities, a test of what counts as a material change, and independent review before it takes effect, including for models that change themselves as new data arrives. In effect from 17 May 2024. Addressed to banks, building societies and designated investment firms; it covers models of all kinds and says nothing about prompts.

items.title: Machine learning principles: 2.3 Manage the full life cycle of models and datasets
items.locator: Part 2: Secure development, principle 2.3, 'Use version-control tools to track and control changes to your software, dataset and resulting model'
items.quote: track which users make changes to datasets and models with full details of any modification (including the author, time and date)
items.why: The most exact official statement of this criterion's third level: changes to datasets and models attributable to a person and a time, reviewed before they are made, and reversible. Principle 2.2 in the same collection adds least privilege, access logging and two-person controls where necessary. Version 2.0, May 2024. Guidance, not a rule, and written before prompts became a common point of change.

items.title: Managing the cyber risk of agentic AI
items.locator: Consideration 4(e) 'Assign and limit an agent's access to credentials' and consideration 5 'Observability'
items.quote: Where possible, logs should be immutable so you can trust them during an investigation.
items.why: Extends access control to the AI system itself: each agent should have its own identity, distinct from any person's, with the fewest permissions and shortest-lived credentials the task allows, and its activity logged where it cannot be altered. Interim advice in a blog post by a named NCSC architect; the page says formal guidance will supersede it.

items.title: Software Security Code of Practice
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.locator: 'Voluntary Software Security Code of Practice', theme 2 'Build environment security', principles 2.1 and 2.2
items.quote: Control and log changes to the build environment.
items.why: What a buyer can ask of the supplier's side of change control: the vendor's senior owner must gain assurance that the environment where the software is built is protected from unauthorised access and that changes to it are controlled and logged. Voluntary, addressed to software vendors and not specific to AI; last updated 15 January 2026.

items.title: How is ChatGPT's behavior changing over time?
items.locator: Abstract on the arXiv record (version 3, 31 October 2023)
items.quote: the behavior of the "same" LLM service can change substantially in a relatively short amount of time
items.why: Measured evidence that a supplier's unannounced update changes what a system does: on one task the same named service fell from 84% to 51% accuracy between March and June 2023. The case for requiring notice of supplier changes and re-testing after them. Cited from the authors' preprint on arXiv; only the abstract was read. Two versions of one supplier's models, on tasks chosen by the authors.

items.title: Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems
items.publisher: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 28 (Sculley and others, Google)
items.locator: Section 2, 'Entanglement', PDF p. 2
items.quote: CACE applies not only to input signals, but also to hyper-parameters, learning settings, sampling methods, convergence thresholds, data selection
items.why: The standard peer-reviewed account of why change control for machine learning must reach beyond code: changing any input, setting or data selection can change everything the system does (the authors' 'changing anything changes everything' principle). Conference paper from the publisher's own proceedings site. Practitioner experience at one company, not a measured study, and it predates language models.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
items.locator: Suggested action MS-2.8-003 under MEASURE 2.8, PDF p. 38; MANAGE 4.1 (change management)
items.quote: Robust version control systems can also be applied to track changes across the AI lifecycle over time.
items.why: International comparator. The US framework's profile for generative AI lists version control and change-management controls among the actions it suggests, alongside a tamper-proof history of content. Voluntary US framework; no legal force in the UK.
